newsitem.title: INDIA: Security men fan out as India state starts strike.
newsitem.headline: Security men fan out as India state starts strike.

text.p: Thousands of armed security men fanned across India's second most populous state on Friday as the ruling party began a general strike to protest against its leader's arrest in a corruption scandal, officials said.
But there was no report of violence so far during the strike in the eastern Bihar state, which was expected to hit shops and businesses but not banks and government offices, they said.
"Police and magistrates have been deployed all over the state at all sensitive points," Chief Secretary B.P. Varma, the state's top civil servant, told Reuters in the capital, Patna.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, a charismatic leader of low castes, began a two-week remand on Wednesday after surrendering to a court in the $280-million "fodder scam" in which federal police have filed corruption charges that the leader vehemently denies.

Yadav, first indicted in April, resigned as chief minister a week ago after a court issued a warrant and failed in his attempts to win "anticipatory bail" to avoid arrest in the scandal involving suspected misuse of farm and animal welfare funds.
Yadav named his unschooled wife, Rabri Devi, as chief minister in a move that sparked protests from the opposition.
Hindu caste animosities and tussles between landlords and peasants often spell violence in the poor state of 93 million people, of whom 61 percent cannot read or write.

"We have paramilitary forces from the central (federal) government and also the Bihar Military Police in small sections," Varma said. "They have arms and batons," he said, but added that guns were a last resort.
"Crowd control is primarily done by lathi (baton)," he said.
An estimated 5,000 paramilitary personnel would stand by to help police and district-level security men, he said.
"The situation is being monitored closely. Till now there has been no untoward incident," Varma said.

India's ruling 15-party United Front coalition has been sharply divided by a debate over corruption and Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has faced criticism over his failure to take firm action against Yadav.
Yadav formed his breakaway Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) party last month alleging irregularities in the leadership elections of Gujral's Janata Dal, which he headed until then.
Politicians say his wife must ensure peace to defuse demands from the opposition, which wants the federal government to dismiss her rule.
The 38-year-old Devi, a mother of nine children, appealed on Thursday to ensure that the "bandh" or general strike, was peaceful, and said her opponents could foment trouble.
She has a tough task in keeping under control faithful followers of her husband, who plan to "fill the jails" from Saturday in his support.

"If needed, we will stop rail, road and air transport. We will not let anything function and force the federal government to set up a special court to try our leader (and secure his release quickly)," RJD labour leader Harilal Bindu told Reuters.
Authorities expected no violence since the ruling party's credibility was at stake. But they took no chances.
"There are certain places where political parties and activists become restive," Varma said.

Yadav, who ruled Bihar for seven years, travelled in a motorcade to court on Wednesday after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal for "anticipatory bail," allowed under Indian law to persons who expect they may be arrested.
